claim: Most phytophagous insect species exhibit a limited diet breadth and specialize on a few or a single host plant.
source: Most phytophagous insect species exhibit a limited diet breadth and specialize on a few or a single host plant.
evidence: This is a general statement about phytophagous insects presented in the abstract, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Some phytophagous species display a remarkably large diet breadth, with host plants spanning several families and many species.
source: In contrast, some species display a remarkably large diet breadth, with host plants spanning several families and many species.
evidence: This is a general statement about dietary generalism in phytophagous insects, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The consumption of biochemically dissimilar diets resulted in a canalized, generic response from generalist individuals.
source: We showed that the consumption of biochemically dissimilar diets resulted in a canalized, generic response from generalist individuals, consistent with the metabolic generalism hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the metabolomic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many diet-specific metabolites were not metabolized and rather accumulated in consumer individuals.
source: We also showed that many diet-specific metabolites, such as those related to the particular color, odor, or taste of diets, were not metabolized, and rather accumulated in consumer individuals, even when probably detrimental to fitness.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the metabolomic analyses showing accumulation of diet-specific compounds.

claim: While individuals were mostly similar across diets, the detection of their particular diet was straightforward.
source: As a result, while individuals were mostly similar across diets, the detection of their particular diet was straightforward.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA and Elastic Net analyses showing both similarity and discriminability of flies.

claim: Dietary generalism may emerge from a passive, opportunistic use of various resources.
source: Our study thus supports the view that dietary generalism may emerge from a passive, opportunistic use of various resources, contrary to more widespread views of an active role of adaptation in this process.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data and represents a speculative conclusion about the mechanism of dietary generalism.

claim: The vast majority of phytophagous insect species are specialists of one family of plants.
source: In this group, the vast majority of species are specialists of one family of plants (Forister et al., 2015) and this specialization is often accompanied by extreme morphological and/or physiological specializations to exploit a particular plant (e.g. Berenbaum, 1981; Hotti and Rischer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some rarer phytophagous species display a much wider niche breadth, allowing them to consume up to several dozen plant families.
source: In contrast, some rarer species display a much wider niche breadth, allowing them to consume up to several dozen plant families (Clarke et al., 2005; Forister et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transitions between specialism and generalism are bidirectional.
source: The larger proportion of specialists than generalist species (Forister et al., 2015), as well as the fact that transitions between specialism and generalism, are bidirectional (Day et al., 2016; Janz et al., 2001; Nosil, 2002; Nylin et al., 2014), raises questions about the origin and maintenance of generalism (Forister et al., 2012; Singer, 2008), and its biochemical basis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Drosophila suzukii displays an exceptional diet breadth of over 20 plant families.
source: The invasive Drosophila suzukii (the spotted wing Drosophila) displays an exceptional diet breadth of over 20 plant families (Asplen et al., 2015; Bellamy et al., 2013; Cini et al., 2014; Kanzawa, 1939; Kenis et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Poyet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Different diets have an influence on Drosophila suzukii larval development.
source: While multiple experimental studies have found that different diets have an influence on its larval development (Kenis et al., 2016; Olazcuaga et al., 2019; Poyet et al., 2015), it is widely accepted that D. suzukii is a diet generalist species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: The untargeted metabolomics approach enabled the detection and relative quantification of 11,470 unique ions.
source: Our untargeted approach enabled the detection and relative quantification of a set of 11,470 unique ions that were found in at least one fruit or fly sample.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the UHPLC-MS analysis.

claim: The four investigated fruits were biochemically dissimilar.
source: This analysis showed that the four investigated fruits were dissimilar and that technical replicates were highly similar (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Blackcurrant was very dissimilar to all other fruit, discriminated on the first dimension of the PCA explaining 35% of the fruit dataset variance.
source: Blackcurrant was very dissimilar to all other fruit (discriminated on the first dimension of the PCA explaining 35% of the fruit dataset variance).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data.

claim: Cherry was discriminated by the second dimension of the PCA explaining 28% variance.
source: Cherry was then discriminated by the second dimension of the PCA (28% variance explained), and cranberry and strawberry by the third dimension of the PCA (25% variance explained).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data.

claim: Cranberry and strawberry were discriminated by the third dimension of the PCA explaining 25% variance.
source: Cherry was then discriminated by the second dimension of the PCA (28% variance explained), and cranberry and strawberry by the third dimension of the PCA (25% variance explained).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data.

claim: Qualitative data alone enabled perfect discrimination between fruit, with several hundred ions diagnostic of each investigated fruit.
source: Furthermore, while most of the ions were shared among fruits, qualitative data alone enabled perfect discrimination between fruit, with several hundred ions diagnostic of each investigated fruit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by qualitative analysis data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Taxonomic classification was not predictive of chemical proximity between fruits.
source: A simple visual comparison of topologies between this clustering and the corresponding phylogenetic tree of fruit species indicated that taxonomic classification was not predictive of chemical proximity between fruits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis compared to phylogenetic relationships.

claim: There was no correlation between ion quantities in fruits and flies that consumed them.
source: The absence of direct contamination was confirmed by the absence of correlation between ion quantities in fruits and flies that consumed them (all Kendall's τ<0.2; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis data.

claim: Most ions are shared between large groups of fruits and flies.
source: Comparison of the overall intersections of ions present in the different fruits and the flies grown over these fruits showed that most ions are shared between large groups of fruits and flies (i.e. with higher degrees of intersection; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by intersection analysis data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The largest intersection includes 3691 ions shared by all fruits and all flies, representing 32% of detected ions.
source: The largest intersection includes 3691 ions shared by all fruits and all flies (32%).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection analysis.

claim: The second largest intersection comprises 1103 ions shared among all flies and absent in fruits, representing 10% of detected ions.
source: The second largest intersection comprises 1103 ions shared among all flies (and absent in fruits; 10%).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection analysis.

claim: The fourth largest intersection contains 412 ions shared among all fruits and no flies, representing 4% of detected ions.
source: The fourth largest intersection contains 412 ions shared among all fruits (and no flies; 4%).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection analysis.

claim: Ions found uniquely in flies raised on a particular diet are rare.
source: While ions found uniquely in each fruit are not uncommon (>100 ions for all fruits), ions found uniquely in flies raised on a particular diet are rare (two in cherry-fed flies, seven in cranberry-fed flies, and none in strawberry-fed and blackcurrant-fed flies).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection analysis.

claim: Ions that are distinctive of a particular fruit-fly pair are seldom, ranging from 69 in the blackcurrant fruit-fly pair to only seven in the strawberry fruit-fly pair.
source: Ions that are distinctive of a particular fruit-fly pair are also seldom, ranging from 69 in the blackcurrant fruit-fly pair to only seven in the strawberry fruit-fly pair.
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection analysis.

claim: The intersection of all fruits is largely formed from ions common to all fruits, representing 48.6% of all ions present in fruits.
source: First, the intersection of all fruits (left column) is largely formed from ions common to all fruits (48.6% of all ions present in fruits).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection degree analysis.

claim: The intersection degrees of flies show a higher proportion of metabolites common to all flies at 76.3% of all ions present in flies.
source: Second, the intersection degrees of flies show marked differences from those of the fruits (Figure 3, right column). These include a higher proportion of metabolites common to all flies (76.3% of all ions present in flies), smaller proportions of lower degree intersections (intersections of degrees 3, 2, and 1 represent 10.6%, 4%, and 9% of all ions present in flies, respectively), and a large proportion of fruit metabolites that are absent in flies (19.5% of all detected ions).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection degree analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 92% of ions that were present in flies but not in any fruit are ions common to all flies regardless of their diet.
source: It is important to note that 92% of ions that were present in flies but not in any fruit (i.e. derived from de novo produced metabolites; yellow stack, left column) are ions common to all flies regardless of their diet (Figure 3, yellow flow from 0 to 4).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection degree analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 39.4% of ions unique to a given fruit are found in all flies.
source: This includes ions unique to a given fruit, 39.4% of which are found in all flies.
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection degree analysis.

claim: All flies' samples cluster together and away from fruits, regardless of their diets.
source: Results of the PCA show that while different fruits are easily discriminated, differently-fed flies all clustered into a single group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The metabolomes of flies fed on different fruits are mostly identical from a qualitative standpoint.
source: Altogether, our analyses underscore that the metabolomes of flies fed on different fruits are mostly identical, especially from a qualitative standpoint, and unanimously point to metabolic generalism, over multi-host metabolic specialism, as a mechanism promoting diet breadth.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple analyses presented in the results.

claim: Flies' diets can be readily inferred from their metabolomes using PCA.
source: A PCA focusing on the fly dataset demonstrated that flies' diets can be readily inferred (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The first dimension of the PCA on fly data explains 20% of variance and discriminates between biological replicates.
source: While the first dimension of the PCA (20% of variance explained) discriminates between biological replicates of our experiment (i.e. generations of flies), the second and third dimensions of the PCA (18.3% and 10.5% of variance explained, respectively) discriminate fly metabolomes according to their diet.
evidence: This is a direct report of PCA analysis results.

claim: The second and third dimensions of the PCA explain 18.3% and 10.5% of variance respectively and discriminate fly metabolomes according to their diet.
source: While the first dimension of the PCA (20% of variance explained) discriminates between biological replicates of our experiment (i.e. generations of flies), the second and third dimensions of the PCA (18.3% and 10.5% of variance explained, respectively) discriminate fly metabolomes according to their diet.
evidence: This is a direct report of PCA analysis results.

claim: The 'large' list of Elastic Net models enabled a perfect classification of flies according to their diet with ratio of deviance explained >98%.
source: This statistical approach yielded a 'large' list consisting of 169 fly ions associated with a blackcurrant diet, 103 with a cherry diet, 121 with a cranberry diet, and 40 with a strawberry diet. All four 'large' models enabled a perfect classification of flies according to their diet (ratio of deviance explained >98%).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical modeling results.

claim: The 'compact' Elastic Net list yielded 62 fly ions associated with blackcurrant diet, 40 with cherry diet, 49 with cranberry diet, and 15 with strawberry diet.
source: The 'compact' set of Elastic Net parameters attained a similar deviance ratio and yielded a list of 62 fly ions associated with a blackcurrant diet, 40 with a cherry diet, 49 with a cranberry diet, and 15 with a strawberry diet.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical modeling results.

claim: Ions of the 'large' list for a given flies' diet were significantly more present in flies of the said diet than in flies developed on other diets.
source: Consistent with these results, we verified that ions of the 'large' list for a given flies' diet were significantly more present in flies of the said diet than in flies developed on other diets and also more present in the said fruit than on other fruits (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap resampling analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Few diet-specific ions were produced de novo by flies.
source: It is worth noting that few diet-specific ions were produced de novo by flies (fruits intersection of degree zero: 0%, 5%, 5%, and 3% ions in blackcurrant, cherry, cranberry, and strawberry-fed flies, respectively), consistent with the metabolic generalism hypothesis.
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from the intersection analysis.

claim: Quantitative levels of ions are critical to correctly classify fly metabolomes according to diet.
source: Altogether, we found that quantitative levels of ions are critical to correctly classify fly metabolomes according to diet.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the classification analyses.

claim: Randomly picking ~300 ions would lead to a 75% classification accuracy for flies' diet when using their quantification levels.
source: While randomly picking ~300 ions would lead to a 75% classification accuracy for flies' diet when using their quantification levels, a similar performance was attained with a sampling of ~1000 ions when using only their presence.
evidence: This is a direct report of classification analysis results.

claim: Manual curation and detailed mass spectra analysis allowed identification of 71 metabolites, 26 of which were confirmed with commercial standards.
source: Manual curation and detailed mass spectra analysis allowed us to identify 71 metabolites, 26 of which were confirmed with commercial standards.
evidence: This is a direct report of metabolite identification results.

claim: Identified metabolites belonged to major plant metabolite families, including anthocyanins, flavonoids, organic and hydroxycinnamic acids, and terpenes.
source: Identified metabolites belonged to major plant metabolite families, including anthocyanins, flavonoids, organic and hydroxycinnamic acids, and terpenes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of metabolite identification results.

claim: Many of the metabolites identified in specific fruits had already been detected and identified in the same fruits in published literature.
source: A survey of the published literature showed that many of the metabolites identified here in specific fruits (and flies that were grown on them) had already been detected and identified in the same fruits (Figure 5, Supplementary file 1), thereby supporting their correct identification.
evidence: This claim is supported by literature survey and comparison with published data.

claim: Some major fruit metabolites, such as anthocyanins, were detected in flies with relatively low relative abundance (fly/fruit ratio between 0.01 and 0.001).
source: Indeed, some major fruit metabolites, such as the anthocyanins delphinidin in blackcurrant, cyanidin in cherry, or pelargonidin in strawberry, were detected in flies, albeit with a relatively low relative abundance (fly/fruit ratio between 0.01 and 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative metabolite data.

claim: Some less abundant fruit metabolites, such as terpenes, were relatively abundant in flies (fly/fruit ratio >0.5).
source: Conversely, other less abundant fruit metabolites, such as terpenes, were relatively abundant in flies (fly/fruit ratio >0.5).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative metabolite data.

claim: Only some fruit metabolites are metabolized or excreted, while others tend to accumulate in flies.
source: Despite the relatively low number of identified metabolites, our quantification results demonstrate that only some fruit metabolites are metabolized (or excreted), while others tend to accumulate in flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on quantitative metabolite data.

claim: Organic acids tended to be shared by all fruits, but with a particular balance depending on fruits.
source: As expected from previous studies, organic acids tended to be shared by all fruits, but with a particular balance depending on fruits: malic, quinic, and citric acids were always present in fruits (and flies) but with elevated levels in cherry, cranberry, and blackcurrant fruits (and flies that consumed them), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite identification and quantification data.

claim: Strawberry-fed flies displayed elevated levels of pelargonidin glucoside, the main anthocyanin of strawberry fruits.
source: Strawberry-fed flies displayed elevated levels of pelargonidin glucoside, the main anthocyanin of strawberry fruits (da Silva et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite quantification data and citation to published literature.

claim: Cranberry- and cherry-fed flies presented high levels of cyanidin arabinoside, and cyanidin glucoside and rutinoside, the main anthocyanins found in cranberry and cherry, respectively.
source: Similarly, cranberry- and cherry-fed flies presented high levels of cyanidin arabinoside, and cyanidin glucoside and rutinoside, the main anthocyanins found in cranberry and cherry, respectively (Acero et al., 2019; Seeram et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite quantification data and citations to published literature.

claim: Blackcurrant-fed flies can easily be discriminated by their levels in some linalool derivatives.
source: Our results show that blackcurrant-fed flies can easily be discriminated by their levels in some linalool derivatives.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite quantification and discrimination analysis data.

claim: Flies that developed on strawberry can be differentiated based on their elevated content in nerolidol.
source: Similarly, flies that developed on strawberry can be differentiated based on their elevated content in nerolidol, a sesquiterpene found in the floral scent of many plant families (Knudsen et al., 2006) and in fruits including strawberry (Aharoni et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite quantification data and citations to published literature.

claim: Elevated levels of hippuric acid were found in all flies, and particularly in cranberry-fed flies.
source: Indeed, we found elevated levels of hippuric acid in all flies, and particularly in cranberry-fed flies.
evidence: This is a direct report of metabolite quantification data.

claim: Hippuric acid originates from the metabolization of various phenolic compounds by the gut microbiome and is a biomarker of fruit consumption in various species including humans.
source: Hippuric acid originates from the metabolization of various phenolic compounds (such as flavonoids and chlorogenic acids) by the gut microbiome and is a biomarker of fruit (and especially berries) consumption in various species including humans (De Simone et al., 2021; Ulaszewska et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both cherry puree and cherry-fed flies were found to contain amygdalin.
source: Both cherry puree and cherry-fed flies were found to contain amygdalin, which belongs to the cyanogenic glucoside family.
evidence: This is a direct report of metabolite identification data.

claim: Cherry has been identified as an excellent host for D. suzukii in both oviposition preference and larval performance experiments.
source: However, cherry has been identified as an excellent host for D. suzukii, in both oviposition preference and larval performance experiments (Olazcuaga et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published experimental study.

claim: The direct comparison of metabolomes of fruits and individuals that were grown on them sheds light on basic issues pertaining to diet generalism.
source: The direct comparison of metabolomes of fruits and of individuals that were grown on them sheds some light on basic issues pertaining to diet generalism (Forister et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution, with citation to relevant literature.

claim: Consumption by generalist individuals of dissimilar diets resulted in a diet-unspecific qualitative response to host biochemistry.
source: Indeed, we found that consumption by generalist individuals of dissimilar diets resulted in a diet-unspecific qualitative response to host biochemistry, i.e., 'metabolic generalism.'
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The tolerant reaction to diet leads to the passive accumulation of diet-specific metabolites in individuals.
source: This tolerant reaction to diet also leads to the passive accumulation of diet-specific metabolites in individuals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the metabolite accumulation data presented.

claim: The phylogenetic classification of the studied fruit species does not represent their proximity in terms of chemical composition.
source: It is important to note, however, that the phylogenetic classification of the studied fruit species does not represent their proximity in terms of chemical composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the hierarchical clustering analysis compared to phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Individuals showed a remarkably fixed qualitative chemical response to diet, coherent with a canalized response.
source: On the one hand, individuals showed a remarkably fixed qualitative chemical response to diet, coherent with a canalized response.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the qualitative metabolomic data.

claim: Different diets had a significant impact on the quantity of a multitude of ions, resulting in the straightforward identification of insects' diets based on their metabolome.
source: On the other hand, different diets had a significant impact on the quantity of a multitude of ions, resulting in the straightforward identification of insects' diets based on their metabolome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the quantitative metabolomic data and classification analyses.

claim: The physiological response to various diets was generic in structure but plastic when relative metabolite amounts were considered.
source: Our study thus highlights that the physiological response to various diets, while generic in structure, was plastic when relative metabolite amounts were considered.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating both qualitative and quantitative findings.

claim: The simultaneous observation of a single general qualitative response and diverse quantitative responses to diets is coherent with the metabolic generalism hypothesis.
source: The simultaneous observation of a single general qualitative response and diverse quantitative responses to diets is coherent with the metabolic generalism hypothesis and may help reconcile paradoxical notions about the consequences of generalism at the organismal level.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Distinctive fruit secondary metabolites, relating to their specific flavor, color, or scent, were accumulated in corresponding individuals.
source: In particular, we observed that distinctive fruit secondary metabolites, relating to their specific flavor (flavonoids), color (anthocyanins), or scent (terpenoids), were accumulated in corresponding individuals, and that very few de novo diet-specific individuals' metabolites were produced.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite identification and quantification data.

claim: Diet generalization could stem from reduced attention to hosts' biochemical peculiarities and a neutral, passive stance towards potential hosts.
source: Our study thus suggests that diet generalization could stem from reduced attention to hosts' biochemical peculiarities and a neutral, passive stance towards potential hosts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The passive accumulation of terpenoids in blackcurrant-fed flies indicates that D. suzukii may not have evolved efficient monoterpene metabolization pathways.
source: Here, the passive accumulation of terpenoids in blackcurrant-fed flies indicates that D. suzukii may not have evolved efficient monoterpene metabolization pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolite accumulation data.

claim: In D. suzukii, a blackcurrant diet causes a relatively high larval mortality and leads to the extinction of the population in only a couple of generations.
source: Indeed, in D. suzukii, a blackcurrant diet causes a relatively high larval mortality and leads to the extinction of the population in only a couple of generations (Olazcuaga et al., 2019; Olazcuaga et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Metabolic generalism may not exclude some adaptations to cope with specific classes of toxic compounds.
source: Therefore, metabolic generalism may not exclude some adaptations to cope with specific classes of toxic compounds, potentially reflecting the ancestral niche of generalist herbivores.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings about amygdalin tolerance.

claim: The accumulation of flavonoids increases the fitness of some phytophagous species.
source: For instance, the accumulation of flavonoids increases the fitness of some phytophagous species (e.g. Polyommatus icarus; Simmonds, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Passive mechanisms of chemical sequestration may be common in generalist species.
source: While chemical sequestration is an active process in specialist species, passive mechanisms may be common in generalist species (Petschenka and Agrawal, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The passive accumulation of plant metabolites may illustrate a greater opportunity for diet generalism due to plant domestication.
source: The passive accumulation of plant metabolites, such as anthocyanins, may also illustrate a greater opportunity for diet generalism due to plant domestication, especially for frugivorous species (Whitehead et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation to relevant literature.

claim: The domestication of cranberry cultivars resulted in lowered plant defenses responses related to the jasmonic acid pathway.
source: For instance, it has been demonstrated that the domestication of cranberry cultivars, by selecting upon anthocyanin-related traits such as ripening and fruit color intensity, resulted in lowered plant defenses responses related to the jasmonic acid pathway (Rodriguez-Saona et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In strawberries, biochemical insect resistance traits correlate negatively with important agronomical traits such as yield.
source: In strawberries, it is known that biochemical insect resistance traits correlate negatively with important agronomical traits such as yield (Hancock et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Blackcurrant domestication mainly focused on plant pathogens and frost resistance for much of its history.
source: On the contrary, blackcurrant domestication mainly focused on plant pathogens and frost resistance for much of its history (Brennan, 2008), and this could explain the high levels of detrimental terpenoids in this species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and inference about terpenoid levels.

claim: Biochemical changes induced by plant domestication are expected to lead to increased diet generalism.
source: Overall, biochemical changes induced by plant domestication are expected to lead to (i) increased diet generalism and (ii) increased levels of non-lethal plant secondary metabolites in herbivores, especially in frugivores.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the discussion of domestication effects.

claim: Metabolomic data might help track the diet of phytophagous insects in the wild.
source: Finally, by showing that fruit-specific metabolites were readily found in metabolomes, our study suggests that metabolomic data might help track the diet of phytophagous insects in the wild (Alberdi et al., 2019; Nielsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative application based on the study findings, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Fruits are specialized organs interacting with multiple species, with detrimental or beneficial impacts to plant fitness.
source: Compared to more general plant tissues, fruits are specialized organs interacting with multiple species, with detrimental or beneficial impacts to plant fitness, and this may have shaped a greater complexity of the chemical landscape in fruits (Cipollini and Levey, 1997).
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge with citation to relevant literature.

claim: The D. suzukii stock population was initiated by sampling ~1000 flies in the region of Montpellier, France in September and October 2016.
source: Our Drosophila suzukii stock population was initiated by sampling ~1000 flies (more than 500 females and 460 males) in the region of Montpellier (France) in September and October 2016.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methods.

claim: Fruit media consisted of a mix of 60% fruit puree and 40% of a simplified, no-sugar, protein-low version of the 'German Food' medium.
source: To allow the development of D. suzukii, fruit media consisted of a mix of 60% (v/v) fruit puree and of 40% (v/v) of a simplified, no-sugar, protein-low version of the 'German Food' medium, an artificial medium classically used in Drosophila laboratories.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methods.

claim: Samples were analyzed using a UHPLC system equipped with a diode array detector.
source: Extracts were analyzed using a UHPLC system (Dionex Ultimate 3000; Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a diode array detector (DAD).
evidence: This is a direct description of the analytical methods.

claim: The liquid chromatography system was coupled to an Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer.
source: The liquid chromatography system was coupled to an Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with an electrospray ionization source operating in positive and negative modes.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analytical methods.

claim: Raw data from all samples were deposited on the Metabolights repository under accession number MTBLS4721.
source: Raw data from all the samples of flies and fruit purees and from methanol as blank control were deposited on the Metabolights repository (Haug et al., 2020) under accession number MTBLS4721 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metabolights/MTBLS4721).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.
